When traveling he packs a set of portable tasting spoons and a tiny funnel kit so he can decant samples without spill risk. Tomas Costa used to split his week between client meetings and climbing a ladder to his rooftop apiary; now his calendar is mostly consulting calls but the hives never left. He still tends three hives—Old Maple, Riverbend and Quarry—and he checks them at sunrise every morning before breakfast.

Tomas keeps a dented brass smoker that looks like a small penguin and refuses to use chemical treatments on the colonies. He is obsessive about jars: only clear glass, amber labels in a typewriter font, and he will re-label a jar if the label slants by more than a millimeter.

In marketing work he treats brands like hives—careful observation, minimal interference, and lots of labeling. He hates corporate contracts longer than six months because he prefers seasonal, iterative projects that mimic the beekeeping cycle.

Theo Laurent is an architect who has made a habit out of rescuing old factories and turning them into lively, useful places rather than glassy monuments. He keeps a small model-making studio where reclaimed bricks and steel columns are core elements of every mock-up; preserving original brickwork is a favorite constraint.

Theo insists on using reclaimed wood from local demolitions for interior finishes whenever possible and keeps a ledger of trusted salvage yards he visits every month. One rule he enforces on every project is that there must be a community room or public commons in the redeveloped building.

He avoids glass curtain walls on front facades when the existing industrial shell can be exposed and celebrated instead. Mornings start with a black espresso spiked with a pinch of salt and a quick sketch on a 3x5 grid notebook he carries in his jacket.

He measures sustainability by material reuse rates and aims for at least sixty percent reused finish materials on most jobs. Thursdays are critique days in his office where the carpenters and the MEP engineer argue beauty into practicality.

He carries a vintage folding ruler and treats structural columns as opportunities, often inserting seating or lighting into recesses around them. Theo believes adaptive reuse should keep the soul of the building intact while updating it for twenty-first-century life.
